reason: Copying the nuclear DNA is necessary for each daughter cell to receive a complete genome.
expectation: The nucleotides will be used to replicate the DNA in the nucleus, though the precise result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Building the spindle also seems necessary for division, but DNA replication is a useful starting point.

effect: The genome is copied, but sister chromatids still need to be separated into the daughter cells.
reaction: The distinction between copying the whole genome and making proteins is useful.
reason: A spindle should help separate the copied chromosomes during division.
expectation: The centrosomes and spindle proteins will form a spindle, though its exact state is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Cell growth also seems necessary, but I want to prepare for chromosome separation first.

effect: The spindle is formed, but the copied chromosomes have not yet been separated.
reaction: The picture makes the spindle's organization clear, though the wonder adds no explanation.
reason: Combining the copied nucleus with the spindle should advance chromosome separation.
expectation: The spindle will interact with the copied chromosomes and may separate the sister chromatids.

alternatives.reason: Building the cell's body also seems necessary, but I want to follow the chromosome division first.

effect: The chromosome sets are separated, but the cell still needs to divide its shared cytoplasm.
reaction: The distinction between chromosome separation and cell division is clear.
reason: This is the only available combination and appears to prepare materials for cell growth.
expectation: The phospholipids and proteins will form material for the growing cell, though the exact result is uncertain.

effect: The phospholipids and proteins formed membrane vesicles that can now be added to the cell.
reaction: The vesicles make a plausible growth route, though the result gives no further explanation.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should help the cell grow before division.
expectation: The vesicles will contribute membrane to the living cell, producing a larger cell ready for a later division step.

effect: The cell has grown and can now be combined with the separated chromosome sets.
reaction: The explanation usefully distinguishes growth from simply splitting the original cell.
reason: This is the only offered combination and brings cell growth together with chromosome separation.
expectation: The enlarged cell and separated chromosome sets will form a division-ready cell, though further steps may be needed to split it.

effect: Two daughter nuclei have formed, but they still share one cytoplasm.
reaction: The picture clearly shows why nuclear division alone does not make two cells.
reason: The only offered combination should use actin and myosin to divide the cell body.
expectation: Actin and myosin will constrict the cell and separate it into two daughter stem cells, though the exact result is uncertain.

effect: The cell has divided into two unspecialized daughter stem cells, each with a complete nuclear genome, completing the goal.
reaction: The final picture and explanation bring the separate growth, chromosome and division steps together clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Separating the chromosome sets was most worthwhile: the explanation distinguished distributing sister chromatids from dividing the cytoplasm.

leastWorthwhile.text: Making membrane vesicles felt less informative: the picture showed their structure, but the result did not explain how they formed.

surprise.text: The copied genome includes noncoding DNA, and its sister chromatids remain together until separation. That clarified how genome copying differs from protein production.

arbitrary.text: Combining phospholipids with new cell proteins to make vesicles had a plausible purpose, but the connection was not explained in the result.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested to see how cells with the same inherited genome develop different structures through gene expression, as the ending suggests.
